tagline: Nine low islands facing a rising sea
overview:
Tuvalu is a nation of nine tiny coral islands and atolls strung across the central Pacific, between Australia and Hawaii. Its total land area is only about 26 km², the fourth-smallest of any country, and no point rises much more than four or five meters above the ocean.

About 11,000 people live in Tuvalu, making it one of the least populated countries in the world. Tuvaluan and English are the official languages. Funafuti, the capital atoll, holds roughly half the population on a ribbon of land so narrow that in places you can see the lagoon on one side and the open ocean on the other.

Tuvalu is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Fishing licenses sold to foreign fleets, money sent home by Tuvaluan sailors, and the country's internet domain name are its main sources of income. Rising seas are a serious and immediate threat to its future.
landAndNature: Each island is a ring or strip of coral built on the rim of a sunken volcano, with sandy soil too poor for most crops; families grow pulaka, a swamp taro, in pits dug down to the freshwater layer. Coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit provide food and materials. Funafuti's lagoon is a conservation area where turtles, reef sharks and hundreds of fish species live, and seabirds nest on uninhabited islets. There are no rivers or streams, so people collect rainwater from roofs in tanks; droughts force emergency water shipments. Because the land is so low, king tides now push seawater up through the porous coral ground, flooding gardens and roads even on clear days, and storm surges reach across whole islets.
peopleAndCulture: Tuvaluans are Polynesian, and life centers on the extended family, the church and the maneapa, an open community hall where island decisions are made, feasts held and visitors welcomed. Fatele is the great communal performance: rows of singers chant while others drum on a wooden box and dancers move faster and faster as the song builds. Fish, coconut, breadfruit and rice are everyday food, cooked in earth ovens for celebrations. Women weave fans, mats and dance skirts from pandanus leaves. Te ano, a game played with two hard balls kept in the air by teams, is a national sport, along with kilikiti, an island version of cricket. Funafuti's airstrip doubles as the town's main playing field between the few flights.
history: Polynesian voyagers settled these atolls around 3,000 years ago, sailing from Samoa and Tonga, and each island kept its own chiefs and traditions. European ships passed from the 1500s onward. In the 1860s Peruvian slave raiders took hundreds of islanders, devastating some communities. Britain declared a protectorate over the Ellice Islands in 1892 and later governed them with the Gilbert Islands as a single colony. American forces built an airstrip on Funafuti in World War II. In 1974 Ellice Islanders voted to separate from the Gilberts, and Tuvalu became independent on October 1, 1978. In 2000 the country leased its .tv internet address, which brought in significant income. Tuvalu has since become a leading voice at international climate talks, arguing that rising seas threaten its existence.
funFacts: Tuvalu earns millions of dollars a year by leasing its internet domain, .tv, to video and streaming websites.
Funafuti's airport runway becomes a public space between flights, used for soccer, volleyball and evening strolls.
Tuvalu is the least visited country in the world, with only a few thousand tourists arriving in a typical year.
The highest natural point in Tuvalu is only about 4.6 meters above sea level.
Tuvalu has begun creating a digital record of its land, culture and archives in case its islands become uninhabitable.
